items.stem: The Marshall–Lerner condition states that a depreciation will improve the current account if
options: the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than 1
the sum of the price elasticities is less than 1
items.answer: the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than 1
items.markingKey: |PEDx| + |PEDm| > 1.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain the J-curve effect.
items.answer: Diagram: current account balance on vertical axis, time on horizontal. After a depreciation at t0, the balance falls (import bills rise in domestic currency, volumes slow to adjust) and then rises above its original level as export and import volumes respond, giving a J shape.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: initial worsening and reason; 1 mark: later improvement and reason; 1 mark: diagram [3]

items.stem: Explain why the Marshall–Lerner condition must hold for a depreciation to improve the current account.
items.answer: Depreciation lowers foreign-currency export prices and raises domestic-currency import prices. If demand is inelastic, export volumes rise little and import spending in domestic currency rises; only if combined elasticities exceed 1 do volume changes outweigh price changes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price effects; 1 mark: volume effects; 1 mark: elasticities > 1 [3]

items.stem: The price elasticity of demand for Nordavia’s exports is 0.5 and for its imports is 0.2. Its currency depreciates by 20%. In the long run, what happens to the current account (starting from balance)?
items.answer: The current account worsens
items.markingKey: 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7 < 1: Marshall–Lerner condition not met.

items.stem: Lunaria has exports and imports each worth 400 billion in domestic currency. Its currency depreciates by 20% against all currencies. PED for exports is 0.8 and for imports is 0.7. Assume export prices in domestic currency are unchanged and import prices in foreign currency are unchanged. Calculate the new values of exports and imports in domestic currency and the change in the trade balance, and state whether the Marshall–Lerner condition is met.
items.answer: Exports ≈ 464; imports ≈ 412.8 (domestic price +20%, volume −14%); balance changes by 51.2 billion. M–L condition met (0.8 + 0.7 = 1.5).
items.markingKey: Export volume +0.8×20% [1]; import value = 400 × 1.20 × (1 − 0.14) [2]; balance change [1]; M–L test [1]. (Approximate: small rounding differences accepted.)

items.stem: Westaria has exports and imports each worth 200 billion in domestic currency. Its currency depreciates by 10% against all currencies. PED for exports is 1.2 and for imports is 0.4. Assume export prices in domestic currency are unchanged and import prices in foreign currency are unchanged. Calculate the new values of exports and imports in domestic currency and the change in the trade balance, and state whether the Marshall–Lerner condition is met.
items.answer: Exports ≈ 224; imports ≈ 211.2 (domestic price +10%, volume −4%); balance changes by 12.8 billion. M–L condition met (1.2 + 0.4 = 1.6).
items.markingKey: Export volume +1.2×10% [1]; import value = 200 × 1.10 × (1 − 0.04) [2]; balance change [1]; M–L test [1]. (Approximate: small rounding differences accepted.)

items.stem: Extract: Marvona has a current account deficit of 4.5% of GDP. The government is considering a 15% devaluation of its fixed exchange rate. Estimated price elasticities of demand are 0.8 for exports and 0.6 for imports in the long run, but much lower in the first year. (a) Explain one expenditure-reducing policy that could be used instead. (b) Explain why a fall in export prices may increase export revenue.
items.answer: (a) Higher taxes/interest rates reduce AD and imports. (b) If demand is price elastic, volume rise outweighs price fall.

items.stem: Extract: Halvoria has a current account deficit of 5.5% of GDP. The government is considering a 15% devaluation of its fixed exchange rate. Estimated price elasticities of demand are 0.8 for exports and 0.6 for imports in the long run, but much lower in the first year. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the likely path of the current account after the devaluation. (b) Explain one expenditure-reducing policy that could be used instead.
items.answer: (a) J-curve: worsens initially due to low short-run elasticities, then improves if M–L condition holds. (b) Higher taxes/interest rates reduce AD and imports.

items.stem: The J-curve effect suggests that after a depreciation the current account
items.answer: first worsens and then improves
items.markingKey: Demand is inelastic in the short run (contracts, habits), more elastic later.

items.stem: Many of Quentara’s imports are bought under contracts fixed in US dollars for 12 months. Explain why a depreciation may worsen its current account at first.
items.answer: Import volumes cannot change quickly, but each dollar now costs more domestic currency, so the import bill rises before export volumes respond: the start of the J-curve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fixed volumes; 1 mark: higher domestic-currency cost [2]

items.stem: Nordavia’s currency depreciated sharply in Q0. Quarter: Q0 (depreciation), Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5; Current account ($bn): -10, -13, -11, -8, -5, -3. Describe the pattern shown, explain why it occurs and calculate the overall change in the current account between Q0 and Q5.
items.answer: J-curve: the balance worsens to -13 in Q1 then improves, ending at -3, an improvement of 7 billion. Short-run inelastic demand means import bills rise before volumes respond; later elasticities rise and the Marshall–Lerner condition is met.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: initial deterioration; 1 mark: later improvement; 1 mark: elasticity explanation; 1 mark: overall change [4]

items.stem: Westaria’s currency depreciated sharply in Q0. Quarter: Q0 (depreciation), Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5; Current account ($bn): -8, -12, -9, -6, -4, 0. Describe the pattern shown, explain why it occurs and calculate the overall change in the current account between Q0 and Q5.
items.answer: J-curve: the balance worsens to -12 in Q1 then improves, ending at 0, an improvement of 8 billion. Short-run inelastic demand means import bills rise before volumes respond; later elasticities rise and the Marshall–Lerner condition is met.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: initial deterioration; 1 mark: later improvement; 1 mark: elasticity explanation; 1 mark: overall change [4]

items.stem: Pelora’s currency depreciated sharply in Q0. Quarter: Q0 (depreciation), Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5; Current account ($bn): -5, -8, -6, -3, 0, 4. Describe the pattern shown, explain why it occurs and calculate the overall change in the current account between Q0 and Q5.
items.answer: J-curve: the balance worsens to -8 in Q1 then improves, ending at 4, an improvement of 9 billion. Short-run inelastic demand means import bills rise before volumes respond; later elasticities rise and the Marshall–Lerner condition is met.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: initial deterioration; 1 mark: later improvement; 1 mark: elasticity explanation; 1 mark: overall change [4]

items.stem: (a) Explain the Marshall–Lerner condition and the J-curve effect. (b) Discuss the extent to which a depreciation of the currency will always improve the current account.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Exports cheaper, imports dearer; improvement if M–L holds. (b) Case for the view: Exports cheaper, imports dearer; improvement if M–L holds. Case against / evaluation: Short-run J-curve, low elasticities, inflation eroding competitiveness, non-price factors, import content of exports. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: An expenditure-switching policy aims to
options: shift spending from imports to domestically produced goods
reduce total spending in the economy
items.answer: shift spending from imports to domestically produced goods
items.markingKey: Depreciation, tariffs, quotas, subsidies to exporters.

items.stem: Explain how supply-side policies could improve the current account in the long run.
items.answer: Higher productivity and innovation reduce unit costs and improve quality, making exports more competitive and domestic goods better substitutes for imports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: productivity/costs; 1 mark: competitiveness of exports and import substitutes [2]

items.stem: Explain why expenditure-reducing policies may be politically unpopular.
items.answer: They lower AD, raising unemployment and slowing growth, so they reduce imports at the cost of lower living standards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower AD; 1 mark: unemployment/growth cost [2]

items.stem: The world price of textiles is $250 per unit. Selmaria imposes a 25% tariff. Calculate the domestic price after the tariff.

Nordavia imports textiles at a world price of $400. Domestic demand is 1,000 units and domestic supply 500 units. A 15% tariff is imposed; PED for textiles is 1.5 and PES for domestic producers is 1. Calculate the new domestic price, quantities demanded and supplied, imports before and after, and tariff revenue. Explain one disadvantage of the tariff.
items.answer: Price $460; Qd 775; Qs 575; imports fall from 500 to 200; tariff revenue $12,000. Disadvantages: higher prices for consumers, inefficient domestic producers protected, retaliation, deadweight losses.
items.markingKey: Price [1]; %ΔQd = −1.5×15% and %ΔQs = 1×15% [2]; imports = Qd − Qs [1]; revenue = imports × tariff per unit ($60) [1]; disadvantage [1].

Estimated price elasticities of demand are 0.8 for exports and 0.6 for imports in the long run, but much lower in the first year. (a) State whether the Marshall–Lerner condition is met. (b) Explain why a fall in export prices may increase export revenue.
items.answer: (a) 0.8 + 0.6 = 1.4: met (b) If demand is price elastic, volume rise outweighs price fall.

items.stem: The central bank of Valdoria raises interest rates. Explain the two opposing effects on the current account.
items.answer: Lower domestic spending reduces imports (improves CA); but higher rates attract hot money, appreciating the currency, making exports dearer and imports cheaper (worsens CA).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each effect [2]

items.stem: The world price of cars is $200 per unit. Dravonia imposes a 10% tariff. Calculate the domestic price after the tariff.
Rovania has a current account deficit of 6% of GDP caused by a consumer boom. Analyse whether expenditure-reducing or expenditure-switching policy would be more appropriate.
items.answer: The cause is excess domestic demand, so expenditure-reducing policy (higher taxes or interest rates) directly reduces imports and inflationary pressure; expenditure switching (depreciation) adds to demand when the economy is already overheating, raising inflation. A combination may be needed if competitiveness is also weak.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diagnosis; 1 mark: expenditure-reducing analysis; 1 mark: switching analysis; 1 mark: judgement [4]

items.stem: A country with a persistent current account surplus could reduce it by
items.answer: allowing its currency to appreciate
items.markingKey: Exports dearer, imports cheaper.

items.stem: A persistent current account surplus may be a problem because
options: it may reflect weak domestic demand and can provoke protectionism by trading partners
items.answer: it may reflect weak domestic demand and can provoke protectionism by trading partners
items.markingKey: Also: inflationary pressure, opportunity cost of lower consumption.

items.stem: Explain two policies a country could use to reduce a current account surplus.
items.answer: Allow currency appreciation; expansionary fiscal policy to raise domestic demand; lower interest rates; removal of import restrictions; policies to reduce high household saving (social safety nets).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Halvoria has GDP of $1,000 billion and a current account surplus of 6% of GDP. Exports are $400 billion. Its currency appreciates by 15% and the price elasticity of demand for its exports is 1. Calculate the surplus in $ billion and the approximate fall in export volumes (valued at the original domestic price). Explain one other policy that could reduce the surplus.
items.answer: Surplus = $60 billion; exports fall by about 15% ≈ $60 billion. Other policy: fiscal expansion or lower saving incentives to raise domestic demand and imports.
items.markingKey: 6% × 1,000 [1]; %Δvolume = 1 × 15% [1]; value [1]; policy explained [2].

items.stem: Jovania has run large current account surpluses based on manufactured exports. Discuss the extent to which a current account surplus is always beneficial for a country.
items.answer: Arguments for: Strong exports, jobs, foreign assets. Arguments against / evaluation: Weak domestic consumption, undervalued currency, protectionist reaction, inflation pressure; opportunity cost of saving abroad. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Explain why a current account surplus could lead to inflation.
items.answer: Net exports add to AD; inflows of foreign currency may increase the domestic money supply if the central bank buys foreign currency to hold the exchange rate down.

Extract: Umbria Nova has a current account deficit of 4.5% of GDP. The government is considering a 15% devaluation of its fixed exchange rate. Estimated price elasticities of demand are 0.4 for exports and 0.3 for imports in the long run, but much lower in the first year. (a) State whether the Marshall–Lerner condition is met. (b) Explain one expenditure-reducing policy that could be used instead.
items.answer: (a) 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7: not met (b) Higher taxes/interest rates reduce AD and imports.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A country with a persistent current account surplus could reduce it by (b) A persistent current account surplus may be a problem because
items.answer: (a) allowing its currency to appreciate (b) it may reflect weak domestic demand and can provoke protectionism by trading partners
items.markingKey: (a) Exports dearer, imports cheaper. (b) Also: inflationary pressure, opportunity cost of lower consumption.

items.stem: Explain how higher government spending on social insurance in Westaria might reduce its current account surplus.
items.answer: Households need to save less for emergencies, so consumption (including imports) rises, raising domestic demand relative to output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: less precautionary saving; 1 mark: higher imports [2]

items.stem: Kestria has GDP of $4,000 billion and a current account surplus of 6% of GDP. Exports are $1200 billion. Its currency appreciates by 20% and the price elasticity of demand for its exports is 0.6. Calculate the surplus in $ billion and the approximate fall in export volumes (valued at the original domestic price). Explain one other policy that could reduce the surplus.
items.answer: Surplus = $240 billion; exports fall by about 12% ≈ $144 billion. Other policy: fiscal expansion or lower saving incentives to raise domestic demand and imports.
items.markingKey: 6% × 4,000 [1]; %Δvolume = 0.6 × 20% [1]; value [1]; policy explained [2].

items.stem: Zentara has GDP of $2,000 billion and a current account surplus of 10% of GDP. Exports are $600 billion. items.answer: Surplus = $200 billion; exports fall by about 15% ≈ $90 billion. Other policy: fiscal expansion or lower saving incentives to raise domestic demand and imports.

items.stem: Extract: Jovania has a current account deficit of 4.5% of GDP. The government is considering a 15% devaluation of its fixed exchange rate. Estimated price elasticities of demand are 0.5 for exports and 0.7 for imports in the long run, but much lower in the first year. (a) Discuss whether devaluation is the best way to reduce the deficit. (b) Explain why a fall in export prices may increase export revenue.
items.answer: (a) Depends on elasticities, inflation (imported), retaliation, competitiveness; supply-side improvements more lasting; expenditure reducing causes unemployment. (b) If demand is price elastic, volume rise outweighs price fall.
